subject: telescope
pitch: A brass explorer's telescope on a wooden tripod. A long tube in polished brass with leather-wrapped sections and engraved rings, a smaller finder scope on top, an eyepiece with a rubber cup, focusing knobs, and a mahogany tripod with brass fittings and a little tray holding a rolled star chart.
reasoning:
A brass telescope on a wooden tripod is a simple prop, so I'm planning to build it as plain geometry without joints, using the builder's primitive shapes and placement helpers available in the SDK.

Actually, safer to pre-rotate geometry myself with rotateX before passing to b.part, avoiding reliance on uncertain aim/dir semantics. I'll design a tripod standing at y=0 with a tilted telescope tube around 35 degrees, using a simple root joint around hip height and a mount joint for attaching parts, scaling the tripod to roughly 1.2m tall with a half-meter tube.

I'm settling on using `at` and `aim` parameters to orient the leg and tube geometry, aiming each piece's axis toward a target point. For materials I'll stick with simple color strings for wood, brass, leather, and rubber rather than risking unfamiliar texture or stripe signatures.

For the tube shapes I'll use three.js LatheGeometry for the flare, eyepiece, and knobs, with points defined along the Y axis. I'm computing the tube's tilted direction vector (about 35° elevation toward +Z) from the pivot point, then placing objective and eyepiece ends as offsets along that direction using a helper function, mounting each cylindrical segment with `at`/`aim` pairs.

I'll finalize the seg() helper for cylinder orientation using midpoint/aim, then start laying out the telescope's parts along its axis: the brass main tube, leather wrap sections at specific intervals, engraved brass rings, and the objective lens cap, each defined by position ranges and radii along the pivot axis.

Working through the front-end details next — the glass objective lens disc, brass collar lathe, dew shield as a flared frustum — then moving to the back end with the eyepiece barrel, its rubber cup, and a focus knob. For the focus knob I'm figuring out how to orient a torus so its hole faces correctly along the tube's axis, since the default orientation doesn't align with my aim-based system.

Beyond that I'm planning a finder scope mounted parallel to the main tube with bracket posts connecting them, and starting to think through the mount assembly with a yoke and altitude axle.

For the mount, I'm working out a tripod head with a brass post rising to an axle at the pivot point, flanking it with cheek plates positioned just outside the tube's radius so they don't intersect it.

Still placing yoke parts...

Now I'm working out the tripod structure: a head plate, then three mahogany legs tapering from top to feet, spread at 120° angles with one facing front, computing leg length from the spread radius and height.

For each leg's tapered cylinder geometry, I'm sorting out that the +Y end after aiming points toward the foot, so the smaller radius belongs at the foot end and the larger at the head end. I'm also adding small brass foot shoes resting exactly at floor level, and brass collar fittings positioned partway down each leg near the top.

Now I'm thinking about adding a little tray holding a rolled star chart — trying to figure out whether it should hang between the legs as a shelf or just sit as a separate prop near the tripod, since at the height where legs are close enough together the tray would be too small to span them without a supporting bracket.

Deciding to just rest the tray directly on the floor nearby: a wooden rectangular tray with brass lip edges, holding a rolled chart cylinder with brass end caps and a ribbon tie, positioned off to the side of the tripod. I'm also working out the eyepiece assembly at the back of the telescope tube, lathing a brass barrel profile with a flaring rubber eyecup, positioning it so the base sits where the tube ends and it extends outward toward where the viewer's eye would be.

Now I'm shaping the objective end of the tube with a flared brass bell lathe profile, defining radius points that taper outward from the barrel into a wider flange cap near the front opening.

I'm picking the color palette next -- brass tones for the fittings, leather and mahogany for the body, dark rubber for the eyepiece cup, deep blue for the lens glass, and cream for paper detailing.

I'm setting up a single root joint for the skeleton structure and planning a perpendicular offset vector to position the finder scope tube alongside the main barrel, verifying the dot product confirms the vectors are orthogonal.

Now I'm working out the telescope's tilt geometry: a 35° elevation angle from a pivot point determines where the front tip and eyepiece end land in space, and I'm cross-checking these coordinates against the tripod leg positions to confirm nothing overlaps -- then placing the tripod head, column, and crossbar heights before verifying the tube pivot and cheek supports don't collide with the head assembly.

I'm positioning the finder scope assembly above the main tube, including its mounting brackets, small front cap, and eyepiece, then defining a focus collar as a torus rotated so its axis aligns with the tube's direction vector.

For the engraved detail rings I'm using thin low-poly toruses positioned along the tube at several points, plus a cylinder helper function that builds leather-wrap segments with correct top/bottom radii matching the tube's taper, orienting each segment via the aim direction between its endpoints.

I'm also sketching generic helpers for arbitrary 3D segments and for lathe profiles, so I can build legs and revolved shapes by just specifying a start point, direction sign, and radius profile, letting the aim vector handle orientation automatically.

For the tripod, I'm defining legs as tapered cylinders from top to foot, adding small brass collar segments partway down, and placing rubber ferrules as vertical cylinders resting at ground level under each foot.

Now I'm working out the vertical stacking for the head assembly: a mahogany pad, brass disc, short column, crossbar, and cheeks, carefully adjusting each piece's y-center and height so they stack flush without gaps.

For the tray accessory, I'm placing it on the floor at a front-right offset, defining its wooden base box and then adding thin brass rim strips along the front/back and side edges to frame it.

Now I'm adding a rolled chart resting in the tray as a horizontal cylinder with brass end caps, plus a small red ribbon box wrapped around it for detail, keeping the texture simple rather than attempting an SVG print. For the telescope itself, I'm settling on a brass main tube, dark leather wrapping, and bronze-toned rings as the color palette.

I'm working out the telescope's segment layout along its length—figuring out where the leather wraps sit, placing a focus collar via torus geometry near the eyepiece end, and building up the eyepiece assembly as a lathe shape for the barrel transitioning into a rubber cup, choosing colors and radii for brass, rubber, and trim as I go.

Now I'm defining the main tube's objective end with a flared bell shape and lens cap using lathe and cylinder primitives, then setting up the finder scope as a separate smaller cylinder offset along the height axis, complete with mounting brackets, an objective cap, and a small eyepiece cylinder near its rear.

I'm fixing a helper function for building tapered cylinder segments between two points (renaming conflicting variable names), assigning mahogany and brass colors for the tripod legs and fittings, and defining a position function that converts along-axis and offset coordinates into 3D points. Now I'm working out the tripod foot placements using angular spacing around the base.

Checking that no legs collide with the telescope tube or accessory tray, since their x/z positions stay clear of the tray's footprint and the tube's path. I'm also setting up engraved decorative rings using a torus helper with slightly darker brass coloring.

For the focus mechanism, I'm adding a small brass knob sphere near the focus collar torus. For the leather wraps on the tube, I'm building a cylinder-segment helper that creates tapered leather bands at specific positions along the tube, making sure they don't overlap awkwardly with the eyepiece barrel or each other.

I'm defining a lathe geometry helper for revolved shapes like the bell flare and rubber eyecup, carefully choosing profile points so the geometry doesn't degenerate and accounting for which end is open versus covered by the lens cap.

Now I'm working out the finder scope's small barrel, lens, and support brackets, positioning them using the same directional helper so they attach correctly to the main tube's surface.

For the tripod, I'm laying out the mahogany head block, brass mounting plate, crossbar, cheek supports, axle, and small brass knob spheres at the axle ends, checking that none of these pieces clip into each other given their y-positions.

I'm figuring out the three tripod legs running from the head block to foot positions on the ground, adding brass collar bands partway down each leg and rubber ferrule caps at the feet, verifying the geometry stays proportioned relative to the leg length.

For the accessory tray, I'm sizing a wooden box base with a brass rim, then placing a rolled star chart cylinder with end caps and a ribbon tie on top, checking that the chart sits flush on the tray floor.

I'm double-checking that the tilted telescope tube and eyepiece don't collide with the tripod legs or head block given the mounting height and tilt angle, and confirming the overall model's vertical extent from the feet to the tube's front tip.

Now I'm settling on the color palette for brass, dark brass, leather, mahogany, rubber, lens glass, paper, and ribbon materials.

I'm drafting the actual module structure: importing three.js and the builder utility, defining a 3D point type, exporting metadata with a name and description, and setting up the build function that creates the builder, adds a mounting joint, and defines a coordinate helper function that maps a position along the tilted tube axis (plus an optional radial offset) into world space.

Writing geometry helper functions...
